questions.question: A spinner is divided into 4 equal sections coloured red, blue, green, and yellow. What is the probability of one spin landing on blue?
questions.explain: Probability of one outcome = the number of sections for that colour over the total number of equal sections, so blue is 1 out of 4 = 1/4. A common trap is writing 1/3 by comparing blue to the other three colours instead of to the whole spinner.

questions.question: A bag holds 3 red marbles and 5 blue marbles. Without looking, you pull out one marble. What is the probability it is red?
questions.explain: First find the total: 3 + 5 = 8 marbles, so red is 3 out of 8 = 3/8. The most common mistake is writing 3/5, which compares red to blue instead of red to the total.

questions.question: You roll one fair six-sided die. What is the probability of rolling a 4?
questions.explain: A die has 6 equally likely outcomes and only one of them is a 4, so the probability is 1/6. Writing 4/6 is the usual trap — the 4 is the name of the outcome, not how many ways it can happen.

questions.question: A spinner has 6 equal sections. Two of the sections are green and the other four are white. What is the probability of one spin landing on green?
questions.explain: Green covers 2 of the 6 equal sections, so the probability is 2/6 (which is the same as 1/3). Watch out for 2/4, which compares green sections to white sections instead of to all 6 sections.

questions.question: At a Richmond night market, a prize spinner has 10 equal sections: 4 sticker sections, 3 keychain sections, 2 eraser sections, and 1 free-ride section. Maya spins once. What is the probability she wins a keychain?
questions.explain: There are 3 keychain sections out of 10 equal sections in total, so the probability is 3/10. The trap is 3/7, which compares keychain sections to the 7 non-keychain sections instead of to the whole spinner.

questions.question: Owen empties his coin jar and finds 5 toonies, 4 loonies, and 11 quarters. He shakes the jar and pulls out one coin without looking. What is the probability he pulls out a loonie?
questions.explain: Add all the coins first: 5 + 4 + 11 = 20, and 4 of them are loonies, so the probability is 4/20 (= 1/5). A common error is 4/16, which leaves the loonies out of the total instead of counting every coin in the jar.

questions.question: Ava is making a spinner for a class game. She wants the probability of landing on green to be exactly 1/2. Which spinner should she build?
options: A spinner with 8 equal sections, 4 of them green
A spinner with 6 equal sections, 2 of them green
A spinner with 10 equal sections, 3 of them green
A spinner with 4 equal sections, 1 of them green
questions.explain: A probability of 1/2 means green must cover half the equal sections, and 4 out of 8 is exactly half. Students often pick a spinner just because it has more green sections, but you must compare the green sections to the total every time.

questions.question: A bag at a Kelowna school fair holds 4 red counters and 8 blue counters. Kai reaches in, takes out 2 blue counters, and keeps them. He then pulls one more counter without looking. What is the probability this counter is blue?
questions.explain: After 2 blue counters are removed there are 6 blue left and 12 − 2 = 10 counters in the bag, so the probability is 6/10 (= 3/5). The classic trap is 6/12: when counters leave the bag, the total shrinks too.

questions.question: Sofia spins a spinner with 4 equal sections: red, blue, green, and yellow. Her first three spins all land on red. What is the probability that her next spin lands on red?
options: Less than 1/4, because red has already come up three times in a row
3/4, because red came up on 3 of the last spins
1/4, because each spin is an independent event
1/16, because you multiply the chances of the earlier spins together
questions.explain: Spins are independent events — the spinner has no memory, so red is still 1 out of 4 equal sections and the probability stays 1/4. The most common misconception is thinking a colour becomes "due" or "used up" after a streak.

questions.question: A Grade 5 class sells 24 raffle tickets for a Stanley Park field trip. There are 6 blue tickets, 10 red tickets, and the rest are yellow. One ticket is drawn at random. What is the probability that a yellow ticket is drawn?
questions.explain: Find the yellow tickets first: 24 − 6 − 10 = 8, so the probability is 8 out of 24 = 8/24 (= 1/3). The usual trap is 8/16, which compares yellow tickets to the other tickets instead of to all 24.

questions.question: Ethan's spinner has 10 equal sections, and 3 of them are already coloured orange. He wants the probability of landing on orange to be exactly 1/2. How many more sections must he colour orange?
questions.explain: A probability of 1/2 means half of the 10 sections must be orange, which is 5; since 3 are already orange, he needs 5 − 3 = 2 more. The common slip is answering 5 — that is the total number of orange sections needed, not how many more to colour.

questions.question: At the school fair Chloe may draw one token from Bag A or Bag B. Bag A has 3 gold tokens out of 12 tokens. Bag B has 4 gold tokens out of 20 tokens. Which bag gives her the better chance of drawing gold?
options: Bag B, because it has 4 gold tokens and Bag A has only 3
Bag A, because 3 out of 12 is 1/4 and 4 out of 20 is 1/5, and 1/4 is greater than 1/5
Bag B, because 20 tokens is more than 12 tokens
They are equal, because both bags work out to 1/4
questions.explain: Write each chance as a fraction and simplify: 3/12 = 1/4 and 4/20 = 1/5, and 1/4 > 1/5, so Bag A is better. The big misconception is choosing the bag with more gold tokens — probability depends on the gold tokens compared to the total, not the count alone.
